entries.title: Seiya Suzuki’s defense: From ‘a little bit of a worry’ to highlight-reel throw, dependability for Cubs
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS – If I say “Seiya Suzuki” and “defense,” what comes to your minds, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> fans?</p><p>Do you immediately jump to <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wJ5phrfmimM" target="_blank" >the fly ball he dropped in Atlanta</a> at the close of the 2023 season? Does it color your opinion of Suzuki as a defender?</p><p>Maybe Ivan Herrera is in the same camp. After all, the Cardinals catcher chose to take off for third base in the ninth inning Saturday night, likely not thinking Suzuki would throw him out with an on-the-money, highlight-reel chuck from right field.</p><p>But that’s what happened.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Seiya Suzuki makes a PERFECT throw to nab the runner at 3rd! 😮 <a href="https://t.co/GOk7JfB85x">pic.twitter.com/GOk7JfB85x</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2060907385254752651?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 31, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>Maybe it’s about time everyone – fans, opposing players, everyone – realized what kind of defender Suzuki can be.</p><p>“The last few years, with my defense, I think there was a little bit of worry,” Suzuki said through an interpreter following Saturday’s Cubs win. “But coming into this year, I felt good.”</p><p>He’s mostly looked good, too, at least to his teammates, who have noticed someone who has prioritized improving his defense.</p><p>“It’s never been an ability thing,” shortstop Dansby Swanson told the Sun-Times on Sunday. “I think Seiya might have more talent than anybody on our team. Just the things he’s capable of doing, it’s so impressive.</p><p>“For him to be almost humble enough to know he’s got things that he can work on and get better at – and also go work on them and get better at them – kind of shows who he is and how much he cares about his craft and being a good player.”</p><p>That’s a big deal, obviously, for a Cubs team that has built a reputation around playing sensational defense. Swanson is one of five Gold Glovers in the everyday lineup, alongside second baseman Nico Hoerner, third baseman Alex Bregman, left fielder Ian Happ and center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong.</p><p>But just because guys like Suzuki and first baseman Michael Busch aren’t award-winners for their defense doesn’t mean they’re not quality defenders.</p><p>After winning the team Gold Glove last season, the Cubs again rank as the best defensive team in baseball, according to multiple metrics like Outs Above Average and Fielding Run Value.</p><p>They’re flashing leather all over the field, and no opposing hitter or base-runner is safe.</p><p>“It really sets our team up to have a lot of success,” Swanson said, “because when you make other teams earn their way on base, earn their way around the bases, it can make it really, really hard. It can be like a suffocating type of feeling, just because all over the diamond, we have guys that are capable of doing some pretty special things.</p><p>“It is one of our calling cards of this group, our defensive ability.”</p><p>But as impressive as Saturday night’s throw was, as improved a defender as he’s become, Suzuki is here to hit.</p><p>Suzuki came into Sunday batting .250/.339/.405 with seven homers in 45 games. The batting average and on-base percentage actually look better than they did in 2025, but a middle-of-the-order hitter like Suzuki – who hit 32 bombs last year, two off the team lead – is expected to produce more in the power department.</p><p>“There’s good at-bats in there, some bad at-bats. But I think the amount of good at-bats are increasing, and I’m trying to figure everything out one at-bat at a time,” he said. “Even if I’m not hitting well, I can focus on defense and try to help the team there, too. But I’m trying to get that offense going.”</p><p>The total-package version of Suzuki is the kind of player the Cubs can use to achieve their sky-high, championship-level goals. And this might be their last chance to do so; Suzuki is due to hit free agency at the close of the campaign.</p><p>Until then, he’s a critical part of their winning formula – on both sides of the ball.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: What can White Sox rookie David Sandlin do for an encore? How about a no-hitter?
entries.summary: <p>How on earth can White Sox right-hander <b>David Sandlin</b> top his major-league debut, in which he retired 18 consecutive hitters after allowing a leadoff home run?</p><p>‘‘Well, if he doesn’t throw a no-hitter, it might be a failure,’’ Sox pitching coach <b>Zach Bove</b> joked Sunday.</p><p>A no-no certainly would be an improvement, but not by a lot. Sandlin, a 6-4, 220-pounder with a fastball that reached 97.7 mph in the Sox’ 15-2 drubbing of the Twins on Wednesday, will see them again Monday, this time at Target Field.</p><p>Sandlin, 25, handled the Twins like a seasoned pro, allowing one hit — the homer to <b>Byron Buxton</b> — with four strikeouts and no walks in six innings. He threw only 61 pitches, 41 for strikes. And according to Elias, the 18 consecutive batters Sandlin retired were the most by a Sox pitcher in his major-league debut in the last, oh, 100 years.</p><p>‘‘It was great for him to have that success, especially in his debut,’’ Bove said. ‘‘But the next day is like, ‘What went well? What are some things we can do better?’ And then it’s on to the next week.</p><p>‘‘Obviously, he’s facing the same team, so we’re not going to overthink that. He’s kind of familiar with those guys; they’re familiar with him.’’</p><p>Something will have to give, but that hasn’t been a Sox starter lately. Since Sandlin’s debut, <b>Davis Martin</b>, <b>Anthony Kay</b> and <b>Sean Burke</b> allowed one run each in starts of five to six innings. In the other game, opener <b>Brandon Eisert</b> and <b>Erick Fedde</b> combined to allow two runs in 5⅓ innings.</p><h3>Schultz, Smith updates</h3><p>Rookie left-hander <b>Noah Schultz</b>, whom the Sox put on the 15-day injured list (retroactive to last Monday) with tendinitis in his right knee, threw well in the bullpen, Bove said.</p><p>‘‘We’ll see how he recovers and [do] another pen from there,’’ Bove said.</p><p>Bove said Schultz also is using the time to fix some things. He allowed 19 runs spanning 17⅓ innings in his last four starts before going on the IL.</p><p>‘‘We had this sample size at the major-league level with things that worked, with things that haven’t,’’ Bove said. ‘‘It’s a usage thing, No. 1. Specifically, with right-handed hitters, make sure that we’re throwing the right pitches. Working on a couple of the shapes, with his slider, adding a little depth to it. Those are the two big focuses.’’</p><p>Bove also said right-hander <b>Shane Smith</b>, who was the Sox’ Opening Day starter and is now on the IL at Triple-A Charlotte with a strained rotator cuff, resumed throwing last week.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>The Sox put left-hander <b>Tyler Gilbert</b> on the family medical-emergency list and called up lefty <b>Chris Murphy</b>, keeping them with four left-handed relievers. The Sox put Murphy right to work, inserting him in the sixth inning Sunday. He walked three in 1⅓ innings but was bailed out by a double-play grounder and a pickoff that was scored as a caught-stealing.</p><p>• Infielder <b>Jacob Gonzalez</b>, the Sox’ first-round pick in 2023, became their 11th player to make his major-league debut this season. That’s tied for the second-most by a team before June since 1945, according to Elias. The Marlins had 12 before June in 1998.</p><h3>ON DECK</h3><p><b>SOX AT TWINS</b></p><p>Monday: David Sandlin (1-0, 1.50 ERA) vs. Joe Ryan (3-3, 2.94), 6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p>Tuesday: Davis Martin (8-1, 2.00) vs. Connor Prielipp (1-3, 5.13), 6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p>Wednesday: Erick Fedde (0-5, 5.40) vs. Taj Bradley (5-1, 3.21), 12:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox put AL Central woes further behind them with sweep of Tigers
entries.summary: <p>The American League Central is a lovely division to travel through. No city is too far from the others.</p><p>For the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a>, however, playing division rivals the last two years hasn’t been lovely at all.</p><p>In the miserable 2024 season, when the Sox lost a major-league-record 121 games, they went 10-42 against Central foes. They showed a modest improvement last season, going 18-34, but it was their fourth consecutive losing record in the division.</p><p>Look at them now.</p><p>After their 2-1 victory Sunday against the Tigers, the Sox are 11-3 in the division. The result gave them a sweep of the series, their second against a Central team, and came after they took three of four from the Twins.</p><p>You don’t need analytics to know a division title — and the accompanying playoff spot — go through a team’s division. And entering June, the Sox are only a game behind the first-place Guardians, the one division team they have yet to face.</p><p>‘‘These are games that we want,’’ said shortstop Colson Montgomery, who breathed life into a listless Sox offense with a solo home run in the seventh inning that tied the score.</p><p>To already have surpassed its Central victory total from 2024 shows how different this club is — not to mention how subpar the division is. But let’s focus on the Sox’ perspective.</p><p>‘‘Different team, different mindset,’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘We have all the confidence in the world. You gotta have that mindset that you can win, you can beat everybody.’’</p><p>They beat the Tigers on Sunday by seemingly waiting them out. After right-hander Keider Montero held them to two hits in six innings, the Sox exploited a Tigers bullpen that had blown a major-league-high 12 leads in the sixth inning or later.</p><p>‘‘We’ve shown all year that we’re a team that, if they get ahead, you can’t just stop,’’ Montgomery said. ‘‘We’re gonna be one at-bat away.’’</p><p>Montgomery’s homer came with one out against Drew Anderson, who subsequently got ripped for consecutive singles by Chase Meidroth, Jacob Gonzalez — whose first hit came in his big-league debut — and Tristan Peters, whose single put the Sox ahead.</p><p>‘‘I was looking for the changeup,’’ said Peters, who fouled off two fastballs and two curveballs before finally seeing that changeup. ‘‘He liked that pitch the other day when we faced him. I didn’t face him, but I was looking at other guys’ at-bats. So just trying to fight it off until I got my pitch.’’</p><p>The Sox’ bullpen had the opposite effect. After starter Sean Burke allowed one run in 5⅓ innings, Chris Murphy (who was called up Sunday), Brandon Eisert, Bryan Hudson and Tyler Davis combined to hold the Tigers to one hit the rest of the way. Davis earned his first career save. Closer Seranthony Dominguez had pitched in the last two games.</p><p>‘‘We learned last year with one-run games it’s not just about the bullpen; it’s about every phase of the game,’’ manager Will Venable said. ‘‘And as we’ve continued to progress in each of those departments, it’s all amounting to us having a better chance to win these closer games.’’</p><p>The Sox (32-27) are five games above .500 for the first time since Sept. 19, 2022, when they were 76-71. They won 18 games in May, their most in a month since May 2021, when they won 19 — and the Central.</p><p>While beating up on the teams below them is great, the Sox will need to maintain their edge when they finally face the Guardians in a series at Rate Field that begins June 22.</p><p>There’s still a lot of baseball to be played between now and then, including a brutal stretch against the Braves, Dodgers and Yankees. But by the looks of it, the Central is<br>becoming a lovely place for the Sox again.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true"
